source.title: Model Capacity Determines Grokking through Competing Memorisation and Generalisation Speeds

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. It contains some visibly flattened figure content, but the relevant findings are also described in the text and tables.
record.tranche_reason: Trains small Transformers on algorithmic modular-arithmetic datasets and measures training/validation accuracy, generalisation delays, and grokking onset while varying model size and other settings. This directly applies the delayed-generalisation measurement, using modular division as well as a modular-addition sweep.
record.gate_note: The paper reports grokking onset, accuracy timing, and memorisation/generalisation speed results. It also varies training fraction, but those results report onset-prediction calibration rather than whether the optimization delay itself grows as training-set size shrinks. It does not measure circuit formation or removal, naturalistic data, or LLM training. Literature findings cited in the background were not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains small decoder-only Transformers on modular division (and addition) with a 0.5 training fraction. It measures train and validation accuracy timing and the generalisation delay ΔE across model widths, which bears directly on V1 (delayed generalisation on algorithmic data). Its main contribution, the Tmem/Tgen intersection as a predictor of grokking onset, is the study's own predictor. That predictor's calibration statistics are not measures of any listed version. Weight-decay and init-scale sweeps are reported only as predictor residuals, so they do not test V3 or V5.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that on modular arithmetic, grokking onset coincides with the intersection of memorisation and generalisation speeds, at a parameter count above the static capacity threshold. Within each fixed setting the intersection remains predictive, while the calibration offset shifts smoothly with weight decay, depth, training fraction, init scale (more weakly) and operation. It is flat across learning rate within the regime where speed is well defined.
record.recipe_differences: Uses small decoder-only Transformers and train/test accuracy timing on algorithmic modular arithmetic, but focuses on modular division and model-capacity/speed sweeps rather than reproducing the original modular-addition setup. It also includes a modular-addition sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome/predictor calibration varies with initialization scale, weight decay, training fraction, depth, and modular operation. Learning-rate results are stable within the three rates that produce grokking; at 3×10−3 no onset appears within the tested width/epoch range, and at 10−2 training does not saturate. The paper also reports that dropout is fixed in the central sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: The parameter count where the random-label memorisation time and the modular-task generalisation time cross tracks the empirical grokking onset. Reported fit: ρ=0.976, slope 0.985, onset about 30% earlier than predicted. Calibration shifts with weight decay, init scale, training fraction, depth and operation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking onset in model size occurs where memorisation speed overtakes generalisation speed, not at the capacity threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Memorisation time on random labels depends on the capacity fraction f, with Tmem ≈ 12.5·exp(25.1f) and R²=0.978.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Larger models memorise faster as a function of capacity fraction.

record.problems: The study is limited to small Transformers and modular tasks; it does not test naturalistic data or large models. Central onset statistics use about 10 cells per figure and are not cross-validated; the authors state that only large effects are detectable. Capacity curves use a single seed per cell. Several sweeps have incomplete or capped cells, including weight_decay 3.0, high learning rates, and deeper architectures. The paper measures training dynamics and onset but does not inspect learned circuits.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for the training-fraction sweep: it reports onset-prediction residuals and calibration by training fraction, not the optimization delay as a function of training-set size. No rows for depth or modular addition: those sweeps report intersection-prediction calibration, but do not add a result bearing on the listed versions beyond the central grokking/timing results. No cited results from prior work are included.

untested.parts: Whether the delay grows as the training set shrinks. The training-fraction sweep reports only predictor residuals and onset parameter counts, not delay length versus α.
All parts: no circuit analysis and no continuous progress measures.
All parts: no non-algorithmic data. The init-scale and weight-decay sweeps report only predictor calibration, not whether grokking is switched on or off.
All parts: no circuit efficiency or norm measurements, and no critical dataset size or ungrokking.
All parts: learned algorithms are not identified.
All parts: AdamW is fixed throughout, and no float-precision or softmax analysis is done.

missing.what: Empirical grokking onsets (non-zero delay) are still recorded at weight decay 0 and 0.01 for all 6 primes. This bears on whether weight decay is needed for grokking, with dropout 0.2 and AdamW still present.
Grokking onsets occur for modular addition at all 5 primes and at depths up to 10. This extends V1 to another operation and to deeper models.
missing.locator: Appendix E.1 Table 13; Appendix D.1 Table 11

missing.what: Size of the generalisation delay in epochs versus parameter count, per prime. The figure is flattened, but the delays appear to be tens to a few hundred epochs within a 5,000-epoch budget.
The training-fraction sweep shows the onset parameter count depends on α. Delay length versus α is not reported.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked predictor-residual rows to V3 and V5. Those rows measure the study's own onset predictor, not the behaviour named in the versions, so they are relinked to none and their V3 and V5 labels are dropped. The delays in Fig. 1 appear small (tens to a few hundred epochs), much shorter than the original's long delays, but the figure text is flattened. The small-models-don't-grok regime was previously reported by Liu et al. 2022 and Huang et al. 2024. The paper is a preprint.

versions.untested_parts: The paper tests delayed generalisation on modular arithmetic and its relationship to model size and learning speeds. It does not establish that the optimization delay grows as the training set shrinks; the training-fraction sweep reports onset-prediction recalibration, not delay duration versus training-set size.
No circuit-level measurement of gradual algorithm formation or removal of memorising components, and no continuous circuit progress measure anticipating the jump.

Initialization-scale and weight-decay sweeps are tested on algorithmic modular tasks. Non-algorithmic data and a lazy-to-rich transition are not tested; the reported sweeps do not demonstrate that grokking can be switched fully on or off.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data.

Weight decay is varied and grokking onset is measured. The paper does not test whether low norm selects a more efficient circuit, identify such a circuit, or test a critical dataset size or ungrokking below it.
The paper does not identify or compare the algorithms learned across runs.
Learning rate is varied, but adaptive-optimizer instabilities and floating-point/softmax limits are not investigated, nor is a numerical artifact explanation tested.

rows.subject: decoder-only Transformer family (individual model sizes not separated in the text description)
rows.size_stated: Embedding width d swept from 10 to 1000; depth 2 and 1 attention head in the central sweep
rows.operation_detail: Train on modular division and measure training and validation accuracy across model sizes.
rows.measure: Training and validation accuracy timing; generalisation delay ΔE, defined from 99% training accuracy and 98% validation accuracy.
rows.baseline: Small models and intermediate models that generalise immediately (zero delay).
rows.value: The text reports three regimes: small models underfit; intermediate models generalise immediately; larger models exhibit grokking, reaching high training accuracy before high validation accuracy.
rows.uncertainty: ΔE is the per-seed minimum across 10 seeds; no error bar stated for this qualitative result.
rows.note: The paper explicitly describes zero delay at smaller sizes and non-zero delay at larger sizes. Figure 1 also plots delays, but exact per-model values are not given in the text.
rows.check: The row mixes three regimes. The V1 effect (high train accuracy before high validation accuracy) is observed only for larger models. Small models underfit and intermediate models show zero delay. That size dependence is a scope condition, not the baseline. The 'observed' state should be read as applying to the larger-model regime.

source_check.correct: Split by capacity regime: larger models exhibit delayed generalisation (observed); intermediate models generalise immediately with ΔE=0 (absent); small models underfit without exhibiting grokking. A single observed state does not describe the whole family.
source_check.locator_found: Sections 4.3 and 5.3–5.4; Figure 4 caption; Appendix A.6.
source_check.problem: The row combines underfitting, immediate generalisation and delayed generalisation under one observed state.

rows.subject: decoder-only Transformer family (aggregate across primes)
rows.size_stated: Parameter count P varied; individual widths and counts not reported for this aggregate result
rows.operation_detail: Compare the random-label memorisation time Tmem(P) with modular-task generalisation time Tgen(P), and compare their intersection with empirical grokking onset.
rows.measure: Association and calibration between predicted intersection parameter count Pcross and empirical onset Ponset.
rows.value: Spearman ρ = 0.976; Kendall τ = 0.911; log–log slope = 0.985; median log10(Ponset/Pcross) = −0.16. The text says empirical onset is roughly 30% earlier than predicted.
rows.uncertainty: Permutation p < 10−3 for Spearman; Kendall p = 3.0 × 10−5; joint calibration F = 199, p = 1.5 × 10−7; Wilcoxon p = 2.0 × 10−3. The paper notes approximately 10 cells per figure and that the tests are not cross-validated.
rows.note: The paper reports that delays are zero while Tgen < Tmem and become non-zero near the speed intersection. This supports the timing account in the tested modular setting, with a systematic onset offset.
rows.check: This row reports the study's own predictor (Pcross vs Ponset calibration: Spearman, slope, offset), not a rate or size of delayed generalisation. It belongs under fits_no_version.
